name: Bach flower remedies

card.summary: A set of 38 diluted flower essences, plus the combined Rescue Remedy, taken in drops that practitioners use to address emotional states such as stress and nervous tension, which some people link to how calm, rested and presentable they look.
card.aka: Bach flower essences, flower therapy, Rescue Remedy (combination product)
card.note: Alcohol-based drops; systematic reviews of randomised trials have not found effects beyond placebo.

quick.overview:
Bach flower remedies are 38 dilute flower preparations devised by the English physician Edward Bach in the 1930s. Each is matched to an emotional state, for example impatience, worry or self-doubt. The best-known product is Rescue Remedy, a blend of five of them.

In appearance-minded circles the interest is indirect: proponents describe the drops as a way to ease stress, nerves and low mood, which they connect to sleep, skin condition and a more relaxed presence. Systematic reviews of randomised trials, summarised by Edzard Ernst and others, have not found differences from placebo.
quick.how: The remedies are sold as small bottles of liquid in an alcohol and water base, taken as a few drops on the tongue or in water, or sold as sprays and pastilles. Practitioners usually pick one or several remedies to match a person's described mood, and many users keep a bottle of Rescue Remedy for stressful moments. Users typically report using them over days to weeks.
quick.risks: The preparations are extremely dilute and are generally described as safe; the base is usually brandy or another alcohol, which matters for children, people avoiding alcohol and those with alcohol-related conditions. Cancer Research UK states there is no scientific evidence that flower remedies can prevent, control or cure any disease, and clinicians caution that they should not replace treatment for anxiety, depression or other medical conditions.

lead: Bach flower remedies are a system of 38 flower-derived liquid preparations developed by the English physician and former bacteriologist Edward Bach, who completed the set by 1936. Each remedy is assigned to a negative emotional state, such as fear, uncertainty, loneliness, or despondency, and users choose remedies according to how they feel rather than their physical symptoms.[1][2]

People interested in appearance come to the remedies through the idea that emotional state shows on the face and body. Proponents describe the drops as a gentle aid for nerves, rumination and tension, and many looksmaxxing-adjacent wellness routines treat calmer mood as a route to better sleep, less stress-related skin flare-ups and a more relaxed look. This is a claimed, indirect chain; the remedies are not marketed as cosmetic treatments.

The research record consists mostly of small randomised trials on anxiety, ADHD, pain and quality of life, and several systematic reviews. The reviews of randomised, placebo-controlled trials reported no difference from placebo, while some nursing and scope reviews and observational reports describe symptom relief that proponents attribute to the remedies.[3][4][5][6]

chain: Drops matched to an emotional state
Intended to ease stress and nervous tension
Calmer mood, claimed better sleep and relaxed appearance
angle.text: Users take the drops to settle stress or worry, and some link a calmer state with a fresher, more relaxed look. The link to appearance is the user's own inference; the remedies are positioned as emotional support.

infobox: Sold as non-medicinal or homeopathic-style products in many markets

paras: The remedies are made from wild flowers, trees and plants. Bach described two preparation methods: floating flowers in spring water in sunlight, or boiling plant material, then preserving the resulting mother tincture in brandy.[1][7] Stock bottles are then diluted further, and the finished product is taken a few drops at a time.

Bach grouped the 38 remedies into seven categories covering fear, uncertainty, insufficient interest in present circumstances, loneliness, oversensitivity to influences and ideas, despondency or despair, and over-care for others.[1] Rescue Remedy combines five of them: star of Bethlehem, rock rose, impatiens, cherry plum and clematis.[1][7]

Bach trained as a doctor, qualified in 1912, and worked in bacteriology and later at the London Homoeopathic Hospital, where he developed bowel nosodes.[1][7] In 1930 he left his Harley Street practice and travelled through Wales and England identifying flowers by intuition and matching them to emotional states.[1] He published Heal Thyself in 1931 and died in 1936, soon after completing the set.[7] His associates Nora Weeks and Victor Bullen continued the work, and the Bach Centre at Mount Vernon in Oxfordshire remains associated with the system.[1]

Bach and later practitioners describe the remedies as carrying the energetic or vibrational character of a plant, which is said to restore balance in a matching emotional state.[1][7] The dilutions are so high that little or no plant material is expected to remain, and mainstream scientists say no conventional pharmacological mechanism is known.[7]

A 2002 systematic review of controlled trials of flower remedies concluded that rigorous trials did not support an effect beyond placebo.[4] A 2010 systematic review located seven randomised trials, all but one placebo-controlled, and reported that none of the placebo-controlled trials showed efficacy.[3] A 2009 systematic review of Bach remedies for psychological problems and pain reached a similar conclusion for the better-designed trials and described the remedies as probably safe.[5]

Individual trials include a double-blind randomised study of a combination of Bach remedies for test anxiety in 55 subjects[8] and a prospective double-blind study in children with ADHD.[9] A randomised placebo-controlled trial examined flower therapy for anxiety in overweight or obese adults,[10] and a 2026 triple-blind trial in 99 people with advanced cancer tested a nine-essence solution against placebo for hope and quality of life.[11] A 2022 scope review mapping use in adult health care reported that studies of remedies such as Impatiens, Cherry Plum, White Chestnut and Beech described reductions in anxiety, depression, fear and pain, while noting the evidence base is small.[6] A retrospective case analysis of 384 clients reported that 46 percent of those with pain felt it was relieved and about 88 percent of all subjects reported improved emotional outlook, with the authors discussing placebo effects.[12] No trial has examined the remedies for appearance outcomes.

The preparations are generally regarded as safe because of their dilution, and a 1997 nursing review described them as not interfering with other medication.[13] The alcohol base is the main practical consideration. Cancer Research UK states there is no scientific evidence that flower remedies can control or cure disease.[7]

Surveys of complementary-medicine organisations and studies of Latin American adults record that opinions of the remedies are favourable among users and practitioners, and that media coverage of them in Spain has been analysed alongside homeopathy, acupuncture and reiki.[14][15] A French pharmacy-journal critique described the system as a pseudotherapy.[16] Rescue Remedy is sold in pharmacies and health stores in many countries.

timeline.event: Edward Bach qualifies as a doctor.[1]
Bach leaves his Harley Street practice to search for flower remedies.[1]
The set of 38 remedies is complete; Bach dies in November.[1][7]
First systematic review of flower remedy trials.[4]
Systematic review of seven randomised trials.[3]
